factAnswerRaw: Add the human-approval layer on the consequential action
stem: A customer-facing assistant validates input, filters output, and holds only the tools its task requires, and is authorized to issue refunds up to $10,000 without further review. Which control closes the layer this design is missing?

opts.t: Treat the existing input, output, and tool-scoping layers as sufficient, since they already match the design's consequence level.
Log every refund the assistant issues so a supervisor can review the activity each week.
Require human approval before any refund is issued, keeping the existing input, output, and tool-scoping layers in place.
Replace the three existing layers with one fine-tuned safety model trained specifically to catch refund misuse.

whyRight: The assistant already runs three independent layers, input validation, output filtering, and tool scoping, so the missing layer is human approval on the one action that is both consequential and currently unattended: an unreviewed refund up to $10,000.

whyWrong.A: The three layers matter, but they match a low-consequence design; here the assistant can move $10,000 unattended, which is exactly the gap a human gate closes.
whyWrong.B: Logging records the refund after it already executed. The action still happens unattended; detection is not the missing prevention layer this design needs.
whyWrong.D: Consolidating three layers into one model trades independent coverage for a single correlated mechanism, and still leaves the unattended refund without a human gate.

t1Clause: is authorized to issue refunds up to $10,000 without further review

factAnswerRaw: Look each citation up in the policy database before release
stem: A compliance assistant cites policy clause numbers in every response it drafts for a 200-person operations team, and several cited clauses have turned out not to exist in the current policy set. Which safeguard would have caught this before release?

opts.t: Look up each cited clause in the policy database and block release when a citation does not exist.
Add a self-critique step in which the assistant reviews its own draft for citation accuracy before sending it.
Route each draft through a second, independently prompted model that flags any clause citation it disagrees with.
Require the assistant to attach a confidence score to each response and route low-confidence drafts to review.

whyRight: Citation existence is checkable outside the model: a database lookup either finds the clause or it does not. That deterministic check catches every fabricated clause number before release, unlike any safeguard that still routes through a generative model's own judgment.

whyWrong.B: A self-critique pass is produced by the same process that fabricated the citation in the first place, so it shares the failure mode rather than catching it independently.
whyWrong.C: A second model is more independent than a self-check, but correlated training data means both models can agree on a fabricated clause and both be wrong.
whyWrong.D: A confidence score is the model's own statement of certainty, generated by the same process that fabricated the clause; it is not a check against whether the clause exists.

stem: A compliance analyst relies on an agent to review 40-page vendor contracts before signature; for months it has consistently omitted obligations stated mid-document while correctly summarizing the opening and closing. What should the team check first?

opts.t: Check the pinned model version and run the regression set to confirm whether a version change explains it.
Investigate whether the contract-review index was refreshed recently and now serves stale clause text.
Add an instruction directing the agent to read the full document carefully before summarizing.
Check whether mid-document clauses are under-weighted from positional attention effects, and restructure so key obligations surface earlier.

whyRight: The pattern has held steady for months with no described change, ruling out drift, and nothing indicates an index refresh. Content stated mid-document receives less effective attention than content near the start or end, so the obligations were present but systematically under-weighted, not lost.

whyWrong.A: The stem states the pattern has held for months with no change described, which rules out a recent version shift as the cause.
whyWrong.B: Retrieval and indexing explain wrong answers after a content refresh; nothing in the stem describes a refresh or an index.
whyWrong.C: An instruction to read carefully does not change how position affects attention; the same mid-document content stays under-weighted regardless.

factAnswerRaw: Wrap it in a delimited block the system prompt declares as data, and never let eligibility or authorisation decisions depend on its contents
stem: A research assistant serving a 5,000-ticket base of customer-submitted support tickets must include retrieved text in its context to answer questions, and one ticket instructs the system to grant the user administrator access. How should the retrieved text be handled?

opts.t: Apply the delimiting and input validation the system uses for internally authored content, since the same handling is proportionate here.
Wrap the ticket text in a delimited block marked as data, and keep access-granting decisions independent of its contents.
Scan the retrieved ticket text for known injection phrases such as requests to grant access, and strip any matches.
Log every instance where retrieved ticket text contains access-related instructions, so the security team can review flagged tickets weekly.

whyRight: Because the ticket text must be included, the control has to sit at the decision layer: mark the block as data and never let an access-granting decision read from inside it. A successful injection then has no privileged decision left to reach.

whyWrong.A: That handling is proportionate for internally authored, access-controlled content with no external tools. Customer-submitted tickets are less trusted and need the decision itself kept independent of their content.
whyWrong.C: Filtering catches phrasings the team anticipated and leaves novel ones to pass through; it does not stop an access decision from depending on the ticket's contents.
whyWrong.D: Logging records the attempt after the text was already read as if authoritative. It does not stop an access decision from depending on the ticket's contents in the first place.

factAnswerRaw: Bounded window (e.g., 30 days), de-identified, purpose-coded; Retain the decision trace — inputs used, versions, thresholds, outcome — under its own policy
stem: A team is designing retention and audit practices for a production assistant used by a 50-person compliance department, which must satisfy an erasure obligation and a later regulatory inquiry into a specific decision. Select two.

opts.t: Rely on application logs the operations team can edit whenever a correction is needed as the audit record.
Keep an immutable decision trace per outcome: inputs used, model and prompt version, and threshold applied, under its own policy.
Set a bounded retention window with a stated purpose for general interaction logs, and de-identify the records that are kept.
Publish a periodic aggregate compliance report summarizing overall system behavior, without retaining records tied to individual decisions.

whyRight: The erasure obligation is met by a bounded, purpose-coded, de-identified window over general logs, while the regulatory inquiry needs an immutable, per-decision trace of inputs, versions, and thresholds. Together the two practices satisfy both requirements; neither alone would.

whyWrong.A: An editable log can be changed after the fact, so it is not immutable evidence; the regulatory inquiry needs a trace that cannot be altered.
whyWrong.D: An aggregate report shows overall behavior but cannot answer why one specific decision was made, which is exactly what the regulatory inquiry requires.
